mainTopic: Crying out and fasting over public disasters, the story of חוני המעגל, rain on a fast day, and the start of the גמרא on when fasts for rain begin.
overview: The amud opens by finishing the משנה's rules for local disasters. The struck city fasts and cries out. Its neighbors fast but do not cry out, though רבי עקיבא says they cry out but do not fast. The same applies to plague (דבר), which the משנה defines as three deaths on three days in a city of 500 men. Disasters that spread, like blight, locusts, wild animals and war, call for crying out everywhere. A few dangers, like a city under siege or a ship in trouble, call for crying out even on שבת. We cry out for every public trouble except too much rain, which leads into the story of חוני המעגל and שמעון בן שטח's sharp but loving reaction. The משנה then rules on rain that falls during a fast day and tells of רבי טרפון in לוד. The גמרא begins by resolving a contradiction about when fasts start, through רב יהודה and רב נחמן. It then explains 'מכת בצורת', and רב נחמן's statement about bringing food from river to river continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The struck city fasts and cries out, and its neighbors only fast
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא rules that the city with no rain fasts and blows the שופר, while the surrounding towns fast but do not blow.
steps.simpleTranslation: That city fasts and cries out, and all the towns around it fast but do not cry out.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues the case of a single city that got no rain. It tells us who fasts and who 'cries out' (blows the שופר).
steps.deeperAnalysis: The city that is actually suffering does both things: it fasts and it cries out. The neighbors share in the pain by fasting, but they do not cry out, because the trouble is not happening to them.

keyTerms.meaning: fasts
cries out (blows the שׁוֹפָר or calls out in prayer)
its surrounding towns

phrases.english: That city fasts and cries out,
phrases.notes: This is the city from just before, where rain did not fall. 'Crying out' means blowing the שופר.

phrases.english: and all its surrounding areas fast but do not cry out.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: The afflicted city fasts and cries out. The surrounding towns fast but do not cry out.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא says the neighbors cry out but do not fast
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא disagrees about the surrounding towns: they cry out but do not fast.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא says: they cry out but do not fast.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא gives a different ruling for the neighboring towns. He flips what they do.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the תנא קמא, the neighbors fast and do not cry out. רבי עקיבא says the opposite: they cry out and do not fast. Both opinions agree that the struck city itself does both.

keyTerms.meaning: they (the towns) cry out

steps.confusionAlert: רבי עקיבא is only arguing about the surrounding towns. He agrees that the struck city itself both fasts and cries out.

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says:
They cry out but do not fast.
phrases.notes: 'They' means the surrounding towns, not the city itself.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר: מַתְרִיעוֹת וְלֹא מִתְעַנּוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the תנא קמא about what the surrounding towns do.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The surrounding towns cry out but do not fast.

steps.title: The same rule applies to plague and collapsing buildings
steps.stepSummary: The משנה applies the same rule, and the same argument, to a city struck by plague (דבר) or by buildings falling down (מפולת).
steps.simpleTranslation: Likewise, a city that has plague or collapsing buildings: that city fasts and cries out, and all the towns around it fast but do not cry out. רבי עקיבא says: they cry out but do not fast.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה takes two new kinds of disaster and says they work exactly like the drought case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word וכן ('and likewise') tells us the whole earlier set of rules carries over. Even the מחלוקת between the תנא קמא and רבי עקיבא repeats in the same form for plague and for collapsing buildings.

keyTerms.meaning: plague, a deadly disease spreading among people
collapse of buildings or walls
and likewise

phrases.english: And likewise, a city that has in it
pestilence or collapsing buildings,
that city fasts and cries out,
and all its surrounding areas fast but do not cry out.
Rabbi Akiva says:
They cry out but do not fast.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן עִיר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ דֶּבֶר אוֹ מַפּוֹלֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the drought rule and its מחלוקת to plague and collapsing buildings.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Plague and collapsing buildings follow the same rules as drought, including the same מחלוקת.

steps.title: What counts as a plague?
steps.stepSummary: The משנה asks how we define דבר, so we know when a series of deaths counts as a plague.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is considered a plague?
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה stops to ask for a definition. This sets up the next step, which gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the משנה just ruled that a plague calls for fasting and crying out, it needs to tell us where the line is. People die all the time, so not every few deaths count as a plague.

keyTerms.meaning: which is? / what counts as?

phrases.english: What is pestilence?

steps.sheelahInformationSought: How many deaths, over what time, make a plague.

steps.title: Three deaths on three days in a city of 500 men
steps.stepSummary: A city with 500 men fit for army service where three people die on three days in a row has a plague. Anything less is not a plague.
steps.simpleTranslation: A city that sends out 500 foot soldiers, and three dead are taken out of it on three days one after another: that is a plague. Less than that is not a plague.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה answers the question with a clear measurement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule depends on the size of the city (500 men) and on a pattern of deaths (one each day for three days in a row). If there are fewer deaths, or the city is bigger, the deaths are treated as normal and not as a plague.

keyTerms.meaning: foot soldier; men fit for army service
one after another, in a row
less than this

steps.whatToRemember: דבר means 3 deaths on 3 days in a row in a city of 500 men.

phrases.english: A city that sends out five hundred infantrymen,
and three dead were taken out of it
on three days, one after the other,
this is pestilence;
less than this, this is not pestilence.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A plague is three deaths on three days in a row in a city of 500 men. Fewer deaths are not a plague.

steps.title: Disasters that spread call for crying out everywhere
steps.stepSummary: For blight, mildew, locusts, caterpillars, wild beasts and the sword, people cry out in every place, because these troubles travel.
steps.simpleTranslation: For these they cry out in every place: blight, mildew, locusts, caterpillars, dangerous beasts and the sword. They cry out over it because it is a disaster that moves.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה lists a new group of disasters. For these, even far-away places cry out, not only the place that was hit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now, only the struck city fully cried out. These disasters are different because they spread from place to place, so every town is in danger. That is why everyone cries out.

keyTerms.meaning: blight, crops dried out by a hot wind
mildew, a crop disease that turns grain pale
a type of locust that comes in swarms
dangerous wild animals
a disaster that moves and spreads

steps.whyThisMatters: The reason given, that the disaster spreads, explains why some troubles stay local and others concern everyone.

phrases.english: For these they cry out in every place:
for blight, and for mildew,
and for locusts, and for caterpillars,
and for dangerous beasts, and for the sword.
They cry out about it
because it is a calamity that spreads.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Disasters that spread require crying out in every place.

steps.title: The זקנים decree fasts for a little blight and for wolves
steps.stepSummary: A story: the זקנים went from ירושלים to their cities and decreed a fast because a small amount of blight appeared in אשקלון, and another fast because wolves ate two children in עבר הירדן.
steps.simpleTranslation: It happened that elders went down from ירושלים to their cities and decreed a fast because blight the size of an oven's mouth was seen in אשקלון. They also decreed a fast because wolves ate two children in עבר הירדן.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה tells a story that shows the rule about spreading disasters in real life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The blight was tiny and only in one city, yet a fast was decreed in other places. That fits the rule that a spreading disaster concerns everyone. The wolves are an example of the חיה רעה from the list.

keyTerms.meaning: a story, an event that happened
the elders, the leading sages
the size of an oven's opening, a very small amount
the land across the ירדן river

phrases.english: An incident: elders went down
from Jerusalem to their cities,
and decreed a fast because there was seen
blight the size of an oven's mouth in Ashkelon.
And they further decreed a fast
because wolves ate
two children in Transjordan.

steps.raayaObject: The rule that spreading disasters call for a response everywhere, even when the disaster is small.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The זקנים decreed fasts over a small amount of blight in אשקלון and over wolves in עבר הירדן.

steps.title: רבי יוסי says the wolves were only seen
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי says the fast was not decreed because the wolves ate children, but only because they were seen.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי says: not because they ate, but because they were seen.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי disagrees about the wolf story. He says no children were eaten, and the wolves were just seen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If רבי יוסי is right, the fast came even earlier, before anyone was hurt. Simply seeing wild animals where people live was enough to decree a fast.

keyTerms.meaning: they were seen

steps.whatToRemember: For a spreading danger like wild animals, the response can come even before harm is done, at least according to רבי יוסי.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says:
Not because they ate,
but because they were seen.
phrases.notes: The wolves were seen in a place where people live, even though they did not harm anyone.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר: לֹא עַל שֶׁאָכְלוּ, אֶלָּא עַל שֶׁנִּרְאוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different account of the wolf story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The fast was decreed only because wolves were seen, even though no one was harmed.

steps.title: Dangers we cry out for even on שבת
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists three emergencies so urgent that we cry out even on שבת: a city surrounded by enemies, a city threatened by a flooding river, and a ship in danger at sea.
steps.simpleTranslation: For these we cry out even on שבת: for a city surrounded by gentile armies or by a flooding river, and for a ship being tossed around at sea.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה lists the emergencies that are serious enough to cry out over even on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the משנה listed troubles we cry out over on regular days. Now it adds that some dangers threaten lives right now, so we do not wait until after שבת. All three cases are sudden dangers to life.

keyTerms.meaning: We cry out in prayer
On שבת, the day of rest
Gentiles, here meaning an enemy army
A ship being tossed around and in danger of sinking

phrases.english: For these they cry out on Shabbat:
for a city that gentiles have surrounded
or a river,
phrases.notes: He means a river that overflowed its banks and surrounds the city with floodwater.

phrases.english: and for a ship being tossed about at sea.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from which troubles we cry out over in general to which ones are urgent enough to cry out over even on שבת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For a city under siege, a city threatened by a flooding river, and a ship in danger at sea, we cry out even on שבת.

steps.title: רבי יוסי: only to call for help
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי says the crying out on שבת is only to call people to come help, not to cry out in prayer to ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי says: we cry out on שבת to call for help, but not to cry out in prayer.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי narrows the rule from the last step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion lets us cry out on שבת in the usual way. רבי יוסי allows it only as a practical call so that people come and save the endangered ones. Crying out to ה׳ in prayer waits until after שבת.

keyTerms.meaning: For help, meaning to call people to come and rescue
For crying out in prayer to ה׳

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says:
for help, but not for crying out.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר: לְעֶזְרָה וְלֹא לִצְעָקָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the kind of crying out allowed on שבת in step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: On שבת we may only sound a call to bring help, not cry out in prayer.

steps.title: שמעון התימני adds plague, but the חכמים disagree
steps.stepSummary: שמעון התימני wants to add plague to the list of things we cry out over on שבת, but the חכמים do not agree with him.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמעון התימני says: we cry out on שבת even for a plague. The חכמים did not agree with him.
steps.whatsHappening: שמעון התימני tries to add one more case to the שבת list, and the חכמים reject it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A plague is deadly, so שמעון התימני treats it like the other emergencies. The חכמים do not agree, so the list stays at the three cases from step 9.

keyTerms.meaning: Plague, a deadly disease spreading in a city
They did not agree with him

phrases.english: Shimon the Timnite says:
even for plague,
but the Sages did not agree with him.

steps.triggerLanguage: שִׁמְעוֹן הַתִּימְנִי אוֹמֵר: אַף עַל הַדֶּבֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proposes widening the שבת list from step 9, and the חכמים reject it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the חכמים, we do not cry out on שבת for a plague.

steps.title: We cry out for every public trouble except too much rain
steps.stepSummary: The משנה gives a general rule: we cry out over any trouble that may come on the community, except for too much rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: For any trouble that may come upon the community, we cry out, except for too much rain.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה states a broad rule and gives one exception: too much rain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Almost any public danger is a reason to cry out. Too much rain is the exception. Even though it can cause damage, rain is a blessing, and the story that follows explains this attitude.

keyTerms.meaning: A trouble or calamity
The community, the public
Too much rain

steps.confusionAlert: "שֶׁלֹּא תָּבוֹא" sounds like "a trouble that won't come," but it is a polite way of saying "a trouble that may come, ה׳ forbid."

phrases.aramaic: עַל כׇּל צָרָה שֶׁלֹּא תָּבוֹא עַל הַצִּבּוּר
phrases.english: For any trouble that should not come upon the community
phrases.notes: This is a polite way of saying "a trouble that might come." People avoided saying it outright.

phrases.english: they cry out over them,
except for too much rain.

steps.triggerLanguage: עַל כׇּל צָרָה שֶׁלֹּא תָּבוֹא עַל הַצִּבּוּר מַתְרִיעִין עֲלֵיהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the שבת cases to a general rule about all public troubles, with one exception.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: We cry out over every public trouble except too much rain.
steps.whyThisMatters: This exception sets up the whole חוני המעגל story, which shows how hesitant we are to pray against rain.

steps.title: חוני is asked to pray, but no rain falls
steps.stepSummary: The people ask חוני המעגל to pray for rain. He confidently tells them to bring in their clay ovens so the rain won't melt them, but when he prays, no rain falls.
steps.simpleTranslation: It once happened that people said to חוני המעגל: "Pray for rain to fall." He said to them: "Go and bring in the ovens used for the קרבן פסח, so they won't melt." He prayed, and no rain fell.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה starts a story about חוני המעגל. This opening sets up the story, which will connect to the rule about too much rain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חוני is so sure his prayer will be answered that he warns people to protect their clay ovens from the rain. Then the surprise comes: nothing happens. This sets up his unusual next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A story, an incident that happened
Honi the Circle-Drawer, a famous צדיק
Clay ovens used to roast the קרבן פסח
They will melt or dissolve

phrases.english: It once happened that they said to Ḥoni HaMe'aggel,
"Pray that rain should fall."

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם: צְאוּ וְהַכְנִיסוּ תַּנּוּרֵי פְסָחִים
phrases.english: He said to them: "Go out and bring in the Pesach ovens,"
phrases.notes: These ovens were made of clay and stood outside, so heavy rain could ruin them.

phrases.english: "so that they will not melt."
He prayed, and no rain fell.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a story that illustrates the rule that we do not cry out over too much rain.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that we do not cry out over too much rain

steps.title: חוני draws a circle and makes an oath
steps.stepSummary: חוני draws a circle, stands inside it, and swears to ה׳ that he will not move until ה׳ has mercy on His children.
steps.simpleTranslation: What did he do? He drew a circle, stood inside it, and said before ה׳: "Master of the world! Your children have turned to me, because I am like a member of Your household. I swear by Your great name that I will not move from here until You have mercy on Your children."
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues: after the first prayer fails, חוני does something dramatic to insist that ה׳ answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חוני says the people turned to him because he is close to ה׳, "like a member of the household." He uses that closeness to make a bold oath not to leave the circle. The story now waits to see how ה׳ responds.

keyTerms.meaning: He drew a circle
Master of the world, a way of addressing ה׳
A member of the household, someone very close
Swearing, making an oath

phrases.english: What did he do?
He drew a circle and stood inside it,
and said before Him:
"Master of the world!"
"Your children have turned their faces to me,"
"because I am like a member of Your household."
"I swear by Your great name"
"that I will not move from here"
"until You have mercy on Your children."

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה עָשָׂה? עָג עוּגָה וְעָמַד בְּתוֹכָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story after the first prayer failed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: חוני insists on rain by standing in a circle and swearing not to leave until ה׳ has mercy.

steps.title: Too little rain, then too much, then חוני asks for blessed rain
steps.stepSummary: First the rain only drips, then it pours down violently. Each time חוני says this is not what he asked for, and he asks for gentle rain of blessing.
steps.simpleTranslation: The rain began to drip. He said: "This is not what I asked for, but rain to fill the pits, ditches, and caves." It began to come down furiously. He said: "This is not what I asked for, but rain of favor, blessing, and generosity."
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues, and חוני adjusts his request twice until the rain is right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A few drops would not help, so חוני asks for enough rain to fill the water storage for the year. Then the rain comes down so hard that it could cause damage, so he asks for rain that is a blessing. This shows he wants exactly the right kind of rain.

keyTerms.meaning: Dripping in small drops
Pits, ditches and caves used to store water
Furiously, violently
Rain of favor, blessing and generosity

phrases.english: Rain began to drip.
He said: "Not for this did I ask,"
"but for rain to fill pits, ditches, and caves."
It began to fall furiously.
He said: "Not for this did I ask,"
"but for rain of favor, blessing, and generosity."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows ה׳ answering חוני's oath, with חוני refining his request twice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: חוני asks for rain that is enough to help and also gentle enough to be a blessing.

steps.title: The people ask חוני to stop the rain, and he holds back
steps.stepSummary: The rain falls properly but keeps going until the people flee to הר הבית. They ask חוני to pray for it to stop, and he tells them to first check whether אבן הטועין has been washed away.
steps.simpleTranslation: The rain fell properly, until the people left the city of ירושלים and went up to הר הבית because of the rain. They came and said to him: "Just as you prayed for it to fall, pray for it to go away." He said to them: "Go and see if אבן הטועין has been washed away."
steps.whatsHappening: The story reaches the part that connects to the rule: the people want חוני to pray against too much rain, and he holds back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rain is the right kind, but there is so much of it that people must leave their homes. חוני still does not rush to pray against it. He sends them to check whether a huge stone has been washed away, meaning only extreme danger would justify praying against rain. This illustrates the rule in step 12.

keyTerms.meaning: In their proper way
The Temple Mount
The Claimants' Stone, a large stone in ירושלים used for lost-and-found claims
Washed away, wiped out

steps.whatToRemember: We cry out over every public trouble except too much rain. חוני shows this by refusing to pray against the rain unless the flooding is extreme enough to wash away a huge stone.

phrases.english: They fell in their proper way,
until the Jews went out of Jerusalem
to the Temple Mount because of the rain.
phrases.notes: The rain was good, but it did not stop. It flooded the lower city, so people went up to the higher ground.

phrases.english: They came and said to him:
"Just as you prayed for them to fall,"
"so pray that they go away."
He said to them: "Go out and see"
"if the Claimants' Stone has been washed away."
phrases.notes: This was a huge stone in the city. He's hinting that only a flood strong enough to wash it away would justify praying against the rain.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָרְדוּ כְּתִקְנָן, עַד שֶׁיָּצְאוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל מִירוּשָׁלַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The story reaches its point: a request to pray against too much rain, which חוני holds back from.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that we do not cry out over too much rain
steps.raayaSupportSource: חוני's answer about אבן הטועין when asked to stop the rain
steps.whyThisMatters: This is where the story connects to the exception in the משנה: even harmful amounts of rain are not prayed against unless the danger is extreme.

steps.title: שמעון בן שטח's message to חוני
steps.stepSummary: שמעון בן שטח tells חוני he deserves נידוי for how he spoke to ה׳, but he cannot do it, because ה׳ treats חוני like a beloved, pampered son.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמעון בן שטח sent a message to חוני: 'If you were not חוני, I would put you in נידוי. But what can I do to you? You nag ה׳ and He gives you what you want, like a son who nags his father and the father gives in. About you the פסוק says: Let your father and mother be glad, and let her who bore you rejoice.'
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה ends the חוני story with the reaction of the leading sage, שמעון בן שטח. He criticizes how חוני acted, yet holds back from punishing him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חוני swore he would not move and kept rejecting the rain ה׳ sent, which sounds disrespectful. That is why שמעון בן שטח says it would normally deserve נידוי. But ה׳ answered every request, which shows a special father-and-son closeness, so שמעון בן שטח praises him with a פסוק instead.

keyTerms.meaning: A ban, excommunication from the community
Acts like a pampered child who nags until he gets his way
A name for ה׳

steps.whatToRemember: The חוני story ends with mixed feelings: his way of speaking to ה׳ was too bold for anyone else, but his closeness to ה׳ was real, and his prayers were answered.

phrases.english: Shimon ben Shetach sent to him:
Were you not Choni,
I would decree excommunication upon you.
But what can I do to you,
for you nag like a pampered child before ה׳
and He does what you want for you,
like a son who nags his father
and the father does what he wants for him,
and about you the verse says:
"Let your father and your mother be glad
and let her who bore you rejoice."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the חוני story by giving the sages' judgment on how he prayed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: חוני's bold way of praying would normally deserve נידוי, but his special closeness to ה׳ protects him.

steps.title: Rain during a fast: sunrise is the cut-off
steps.stepSummary: If rain falls during a fast for rain, the first opinion says: before sunrise you don't finish the fast, after sunrise you do.
steps.simpleTranslation: If people were fasting for rain and rain fell before sunrise, they do not finish the fast. If it fell after sunrise, they finish it.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה starts a new practical rule: what happens to a fast for rain if the rain arrives on the fast day itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fast was for rain, so once rain comes the reason to fast is gone. But this first opinion says that once the day has really started (after sunrise), the fast has already taken hold, so you finish it.

keyTerms.meaning: Fasting
Sunrise
They complete the fast until evening

phrases.english: If they were fasting
and rain fell for them,
before sunrise, they do not complete the fast;
after sunrise, they complete it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the story ends, the משנה moves to a new הלכה about fast days.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If rain falls before sunrise, the fast is not completed; if after sunrise, it is completed.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר: midday is the cut-off
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר disagrees and moves the cut-off to midday.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר says: if rain fell before midday, they do not finish the fast. If it fell after midday, they finish it.
steps.whatsHappening: A second opinion in the משנה argues with the first about when the cut-off time is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both opinions agree on the idea that a fast that has gone on long enough should be finished. They argue only about the time: the first opinion says sunrise, while רבי אליעזר says midday, which gives more room to stop the fast.

keyTerms.meaning: Midday

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer says:
before midday, they do not complete the fast;
after midday, they complete it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a dissenting opinion against the rule in step 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי אליעזר, the cut-off for finishing the fast is midday, not sunrise.

steps.title: The story in לוד with רבי טרפון
steps.stepSummary: In לוד, rain fell before midday on a fast day. רבי טרפון told everyone to stop fasting and celebrate, and in the afternoon they said הלל הגדול.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once a fast was declared in לוד, and rain fell before midday. רבי טרפון told them: 'Go eat, drink, and make it a יום טוב.' They did so, and in the afternoon they came back and said הלל הגדול.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה brings a real story that matches רבי אליעזר's view, since the rain came before midday and they did not finish the fast.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The text only says the rain fell before midday. The story is brought to show רבי אליעזר's view, so the point is that they stopped the fast because it was still before midday, even though the day had already started. He also turned the day into a celebration and thanksgiving for the rain.

keyTerms.meaning: A city in ארץ ישראל
A festive, celebration day
Afternoon, toward evening
The 'great הלל', a special song of praise and thanks

steps.whatToRemember: The story in לוד follows רבי אליעזר: rain before midday ends the fast, and the day becomes a celebration of thanks.

phrases.english: There was an incident where they decreed a fast in Lod,
and rain fell for them before midday.
Rabbi Tarfon said to them:

phrases.aramaic: צְאוּ וְאִכְלוּ וּשְׁתוּ וַעֲשׂוּ יוֹם טוֹב,
phrases.english: Go out, eat, drink, and make a festival day,

phrases.aramaic: וְיָצְאוּ וְאָכְלוּ וְשָׁתוּ וְעָשׂוּ יוֹם טוֹב,
phrases.english: and they went out, ate, drank, and made a festival day,
and they came in the afternoon
and recited the Great Hallel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a real-life case that fits רבי אליעזר's opinion in step 19.
steps.raayaObject: רבי אליעזר's view that rain before midday ends the fast
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of רבי טרפון in לוד, where rain fell before midday and the fast was stopped

steps.title: גמרא quotes: fasts are for the first rainfall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by quoting the line from the start of the פרק's משנה: the order of fasts applies to the first rainfall period.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: The משנה said, 'The order of these fasts is stated for the first rainfall period.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins and quotes a line from the משנה. This is a setup: the next step will challenge this line with a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's line sounds like the fasts already start when the first rainfall period passes without rain. The גמרא brings this wording first so it can compare it with another source.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for גמרא, the discussion on the משנה
The order and schedule of the fasts
The first rainfall period of the winter

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not from the רבי טרפון story just before. The גמרא is going back to the opening line of the פרק's משנה.

phrases.english: Gemara:
The order of these fasts
is stated regarding the first rainfall.
phrases.notes: This quotes the first line of this פרק's משנה, from before the חוני story.

steps.triggerLanguage: סֵדֶר תַּעֲנִיּוֹת הָאֵלּוּ הָאָמוּר בִּרְבִיעָה רִאשׁוֹנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The משנה section ends, and the גמרא begins by quoting an earlier line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה says the fast schedule applies to the first rainfall period.

steps.title: A ברייתא says fasting starts only at the third rainfall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא raises a contradiction: a ברייתא says the first and second rainfall periods are only for prayer, and fasting begins only at the third.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a ברייתא contradicts this: 'When the first and second rainfall periods pass, it is time to ask (pray for rain). When the third passes, it is time to fast!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets the ברייתא against the משנה. They seem to disagree about when the fasting begins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה links the fasts to the first rainfall period. The ברייתא says that at the first and second periods we only pray, and fasting starts only at the third. So the two sources seem to clash, and the גמרא will need to resolve it.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And they raised a contradiction': one source is set against another
To ask, meaning to pray for rain
To fast

phrases.english: And they raised a contradiction:
the first and second rainfall periods are for asking,
the third is for fasting!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the משנה line quoted in step 21 with a contradicting ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's statement that the fasts apply to the first rainfall period
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא says the first and second rainfall periods are only for prayer, and fasting begins at the third. This contradicts linking the fasts to the first period.

steps.title: רב יהודה rereads the משנה to solve the contradiction
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה explains that the ordered fasts begin only after all three rainfall periods pass with no rain. If rain fell in the first period but the crops failed, they cry out immediately.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: this is what the משנה means. When does the order of fasts apply? When the first, second and third rainfall periods have passed and no rain fell. But if rain fell in the first period and people planted, and nothing sprouted, or it sprouted and then turned bad, they cry out right away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction from step 22. It does this by explaining what the משנה really meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said fasting starts only at the third rainfall period. רב יהודה agrees that the regular order of fasts starts only after all three periods pass dry. In his reading the משנה's 'first rainfall' means the whole early rainy season, the first, second and third periods together, and the ordered fasts begin only if none of them brought rain. Rain that came but crops that failed is the second case the משנה teaches. In that case they do not wait at all and cry out immediately.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it means (a rereading of the source)
A rainfall period (there are three in the early rainy season)
They sprouted
They changed (for the worse)
They cry out (sound an alarm in prayer)

steps.confusionAlert: The 'first rainfall' in the משנה stands for the whole early rainy season, all three periods together, so the slow order of fasts starts only after all three pass dry. The case where rain fell but the crops failed is a separate emergency, where they cry out right away.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up two separate tracks: a slow, step-by-step order of fasts for a total lack of rain, and an immediate response when crops are failing.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said: this is what it is saying:
The order of fasts that was stated, when does it apply?
When the first rainfall period has passed
and the second and third, and no rain fell.
But if rain fell in the first rainfall period
and they planted, but nothing sprouted,
or else it sprouted, and then it changed
phrases.notes: 'Changed' means the plants started looking sickly, because no more rain came.

phrases.english: they cry out about them immediately.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in step 22.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to say that fasting begins at the first rainfall period, which clashes with the ברייתא.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ordered fasts start only after all three rainfall periods, which the משנה calls the 'first rainfall', pass dry. If rain fell but the crops failed, they cry out immediately.

steps.title: רב נחמן: only crops that changed, not crops that dried out
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן limits the immediate crying out to crops that turned sickly, not crops that fully dried out.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: this applies specifically if the crops changed. But if they dried out, they do not cry out.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן adds a limit to the rule we just learned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Crops that only look sickly can still be saved, so it makes sense to pray for them. Crops that have fully dried out are lost, so crying out for them would be pointless.

keyTerms.meaning: Specifically, only this case
They dried out

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said: specifically if they changed,
but if they dried out, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the case of 'changed' crops from step 23.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: They cry out only for crops that changed for the worse, not for crops that fully dried out.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious from the משנה's wording?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב נחמן needed to say this, since the משנה already says 'changed'.
steps.simpleTranslation: That's obvious! We learned 'changed' in the משנה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב נחמן: his point seems to add nothing new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The source already uses the word 'changed', not 'dried out'. So the limit seems built into the text, and רב נחמן's statement looks unneeded.

keyTerms.meaning: It's obvious!

phrases.english: That's obvious! We learned 'changed'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether step 24 adds anything new.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's own word 'changed' already rules out crops that dried out, so the statement adds nothing.

steps.title: The new point is about dried crops that grew stalks
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן's point is needed for dried crops that later grew stalks. You might think that growth gives hope, so he teaches that it does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a case where they grew stalks. You might have said that growing stalks counts for something. So he teaches us that it does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by showing the new case רב נחמן is teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the crops dried out but then put out stalks. We might think this shows they are recovering and can be saved through prayer. רב נחמן teaches that they still count as dried out, so they do not cry out.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for (a special case)
Grew stalks / the growing of stalks
You might have said
He teaches us (that it is not so)

steps.whatToRemember: Crops that only look sickly are worth crying out for. Crops that dried out are not, even if they later grew stalks.

phrases.english: No, it is needed where they grew stalks.
You might have said: growing stalks is something meaningful,
phrases.notes: He means: you might think the stalks show the crops are coming back to life.

phrases.english: so he teaches us that it is not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Pointing to a specific case (לא צריכא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Dried crops that grew stalks might count as recovering, so we would cry out for them.
steps.terutzMaskana: Growing stalks does not matter. Such crops still count as dried out, and we do not cry out.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: rain stopped between rainfalls
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה, about rain stopping between one rainfall and the next.
steps.simpleTranslation: And likewise, if rain stopped between one rainfall and another, etc.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next discussion by quoting a new line from the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The full line in the משנה says: if rain stopped for forty days between rainfalls, they cry out, because it is a 'plague of drought'. The גמרא will now explain that last phrase.

keyTerms.meaning: They stopped
Etc. (the rest of the quoted line)

phrases.english: And likewise, if the rains stopped
between one rainfall and another, etc.
phrases.notes: The 'etc.' stands for the rest of the משנה's line: forty days without rain, so they cry out, because it is a plague of drought.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן שֶׁפָּסְקוּ גְּשָׁמִים בֵּין גֶּשֶׁם לְגֶשֶׁם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a new line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A forty-day break in rain between rainfalls is a reason to cry out.

steps.title: What does 'plague of drought' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the משנה means by 'מכת בצורת'.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is a 'plague of drought'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question to explain a phrase in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A forty-day break between rainfalls is not yet a full drought. So the גמרא wants to know why the משנה calls it a 'plague of drought'.

keyTerms.meaning: A plague of drought

phrases.english: What is a 'plague of drought'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a phrase in the משנה line quoted in step 27.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of the phrase 'מכת בצורת'.

steps.title: A plague that leads to drought
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה, quoting רב, explains that it is a plague that leads to drought.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: a plague that brings about a drought.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question it just asked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The forty-day break is not the drought itself. It is a warning sign that a drought may be coming, so they cry out now, before it arrives.

keyTerms.meaning: That brings about, leads to

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav:
A plague that brings about a drought.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 28.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'מכת בצורת' means a plague that leads to drought, not the drought itself.

steps.title: רב נחמן begins: river to river
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן begins a statement about bringing food from one river to another. It continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: river to river…
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן starts a new statement that adds to what 'drought' means. This sets up the next move, and his statement finishes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He is starting to describe a drought-like situation: food does not grow in one place and has to be brought in from another place by river. The ruling itself comes on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: From one river to another river

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said: river to river…
phrases.notes: He means food shipped by river from somewhere else, because it didn't grow here. He keeps going on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues explaining what counts as drought, after step 29.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Not finished yet: it describes food that must be brought from river to river, and the ruling comes on the next amud.
